participants.name: Jagdverband 44, Me 262s
participants.note: Galland's six jets from Munich-Riem (his own account, Die Ersten und die Letzten; JV 44's records are still to find)

paras.text: Six Me 262 jets of JV 44, led by Adolf Galland on his last mission, attack a formation of the 17th Bomb Group's B-26s over the Danube at Neuburg, as the 45th Infantry Division crosses the river below. Three records that never mention each other describe the same five minutes: the 106th AAA AW Battalion's history (its batteries fired on the jets), the 189th Field Artillery Battalion's history (it watched from Bergen, just north-west of the town), and the three Missing Air Crew Reports. The German side is Galland's own account, written in 1953; JV 44's records are still to find.
Clocks: the Army's B time and German summer time were both UTC+2. The MACRs' times are as typed.

The aircraft's paths are drawn from `routes.yml`: the bombers' courses as their Missing Air Crew Reports type them, the formation's way in and home as the 432nd Squadron's sketch draws it (the reading of its two lines is ours, from the crews' statements), and the jets' lines from Riem and at 1725, inferred. The 45th Division's G-2 periodic report for the day gives the jets' height and the second jet's course, and puts the two crashes south-east of T5026, a 1 km square of the Army's map grid, by Bergen [[cite:ok45th-5343/p06]].

- The 17th Bomb Group's records for the day: its route as planned, whether it bombed Lechfeld, and a second target one account names, the ammunition dump at Schrobenhausen, 21 km south-south-east of Neuburg (on the courses the forms type there, and about five minutes' flying: it would fit the co-pilot's "five minutes before reaching the target"). The Air Force Historical Research Agency holds them on microfilm, none online: the group's April 1945 history with its war diary (IRIS 78024, reel B0082, frames 1270-1296) and its squadrons' April histories, the 34th (IRIS 43919, reel A0548), the 37th (IRIS 43975, reel A0549), the 95th (IRIS 44876, reel A0572) and the 432nd (IRIS 46759, reel A0614). The First Tactical Air Force's history (IRIS 240253) says nearly all its operations records were destroyed. The group's April history also has a jet attack on 24 April, a fight of its own: JV 44 attacked B-26s near Donauwörth that day and lost Lützow (Baker, 1996). - The escort's combat reports: Finnegan's probable on Galland and Captain Robert Clark's claim for a second jet, in the 50th Fighter Group's April 1945 history (IRIS 80137, reel B0144, frame 1631). They would put the P-47s on the map. - The fourth B-26, which crash-landed (Ethell), and the six damaged: perhaps the 17th's, perhaps the 42nd Bomb Wing's other groups' (the 320th, and a French group). - JV 44's records and the Luftwaffe's loss returns: which jets were hit, and whether a pilot bailed out (Ethell) or the jet landed (Galland). - The 106th's three "AAA Action Report[s]" of the day, sent at 2225B to the 23d AAA Group, the 45th Division and its artillery [[cite:ok45th-17541/p27]]: not in the museum's collection, so the 23d AAA Group's or the division's files (NARA RG 407).

Galland led six jets from Munich-Riem: "Sechs Düsen-Jäger des J.V. 44 führte ich gegen einen Marauder-Verband ... In der Gegend von Neuburg an der Donau sichtete ich den Verband" (I led six jets of JV 44 against a Marauder formation ... I sighted it in the district of Neuburg on the Danube) [[cite:galland-1953/n385]] [[cite:galland-1953/n386]]. They met it nearly head-on, passed over and wheeled round to attack from behind ([Ethell and Price, 1979, p. 54](https://archive.org/details/germanjetsincomb0000ethe)), as the 37th Squadron's gunners saw No. 25 attacked, "in low from 5 o'clock rear" [[cite:rg92-91150835/p04]]. Galland's rockets did not fire; with his cannon, "Eine Marauder der letzten Kette fliegt brennend und explodierend auseinander. Jetzt greife ich einen weiteren Bomber der voranfliegenden Formation an. Er ist schwer getroffen" (a Marauder of the last flight flies apart, burning and exploding; now I attack another bomber of the leading formation; it is heavily hit) [[cite:galland-1953/n386]]. Kaplan has the first "falling through the formation and colliding with another B-26" ([Kaplan, 2007, pp. 49-50](https://archive.org/details/fighteracesofluf0000kapl)). Of the three Missing Air Crew Reports, only No. 25's describes fire, and Baugher's serial list gives No. 25 to Galland: so his first victim was most likely No. 25, which came down in the woods at Rohrenfels (ours, an inference).

Above the bombers, Lieutenant James Finnegan of the 50th Fighter Group was leading the P-47s' top cover: he saw two jets come up through the formation and two bombers explode, dived on one as it banked left, and fired one three-second burst (Kaplan). Galland, banking steeply left to see whether his second bomber would fall, was hit: knee, instrument panel, both engines. He took his attacker for a Mustang, came down at Riem under a P-47 strafing attack and ran for a bomb crater [[cite:galland-1953/n386]] [[cite:galland-1953/n387]]. Finnegan claimed a probable; in the 1970s a student matched it to Galland from the escort's combat reports, and the two men met in 1979 (Kaplan). Captain Robert Clark of the 50th claimed a second jet, its pilot bailing out (Ethell); Galland says the jet the Americans counted was Leutnant Neumann's, which landed at Riem "voller Treffer" (full of hits) with its pilot unhurt [[cite:galland-1953/n388]].

JV 44 reported five certain kills [[cite:galland-1953/n388]]; Ethell has three B-26s down at once and a fourth so badly damaged it crash-landed. Galland's next paragraph is the ground below: "Der Gegner hatte die Donau, von Norden vordringend, bereits an mehreren Stellen überschritten" (the enemy, pushing from the north, had already crossed the Danube at several places) [[cite:galland-1953/n388]]: the 45th Division's crossings that day.

The B-26s were attacked over a river crossing. On 26 April the 45th Infantry Division crossed the Danube at Neuburg: its command post opened at Rennertshofen at 1010, the 179th Infantry crossed by Ried and fought into the south of Neuburg by evening, and the 157th crossed at Marxheim's blown bridge under 20 mm, mortar and artillery fire [[cite:ok45th-10366/p22]] [[cite:ok45th-10366/p23]] [[cite:ok45th-10366/p24]] [[cite:ok45th-10366/p25]]. The 189th Field Artillery, which Battery D defended, fired from Bergen on vehicles and guns south of the river through the afternoon [[cite:ok45th-10366/p24]]. At 1325, an hour and a half after the jets, the 179th reported three German flak wagons (anti-aircraft guns on carriages) in two map grid squares at the south edge of Neuburg [[cite:ok45th-10366/p23]]; a prisoner taken that evening said the town was held by one company of the 91st Grenadier Replacement Battalion, about 100 men [[cite:ok45th-10366/p25]]. The front on the map is the 12th Army Group's for noon that day, traced: it runs north of Bergen and Wellheim, where the 189th had been since 1015, so at this scale the sheet is behind the day, as the sheets can be (`fronts/README.md`); the division's own reports have the crossing under way through the afternoon.

Three B-26s of the 17th Bomb Group were lost to enemy aircraft over Neuburg between 1145 and 1152, one each from the 34th, 432nd and 37th Squadrons, each with its Missing Air Crew Report [[cite:rg92-91150810/p02]] [[cite:rg92-91150796/p02]] [[cite:rg92-91150835/p02]]; a published account adds a fourth that crash-landed. The 106th AAA AW Battalion's history has its Batteries C and D engaging six Me 262s from 1145B to 1147B "without result" [[cite:ok45th-17560/p06]]; the 189th Field Artillery Battalion's, watching from Bergen, has four jets, three bombers shot down and "one of the German aircraft was downed" [[cite:ok45th-14862/p10]]. Galland's jet was hit by a fighter of the escort (he took it for a Mustang) and he landed it at Riem under attack, his last mission of the war [[cite:galland-1953/n387]]; the fighter was a P-47 by Kaplan's account, not yet checked against the fighter group's record; whose fire, if any, brought down a second, no record read says.
Under Questions and sources, an answer marked *secondary* rests on a published account not yet checked against the record it draws on.

events.words: "Place of Departure Dijon, France ... Target or Intended Destination Lechfeld, Ger.: Type of Mission Bombardment". Big Red's co-pilot, in November: "We were ordered to perform a bombing mission on the German air-field at Lechfele [sic], Germany ... When approximately five minutes before reaching the target, our formation was attacked by German jet propelled fighter planes".
events.source: Missing Air Crew Report 14162, pp. 2, 9
events.note: The other two forms give the same target (MACR 14163, p. 2; MACR 14164, p. 2). Lechfeld is about 65 km south-south-west of Neuburg, bearing about 200°: the courses typed at Neuburg (140°, 155°) point south-south-east, not at it, and five minutes' flying is nearer 30 km than 65. A turn short of the target (an initial point), or a loose recollection; whether the group bombed Lechfeld is not in the records read.

A formation of American bombers flying directly overhead were attacked by four German jet propelled planes, and three of the bombers were shot down, one of which burst into flame and exploded in the air. One of the German aircraft was downed but the rest got away."

claims.question: Which bomber did Galland hit first?
claims.answer: One that caught fire, exploded and fell through the formation, colliding with another B-26; probably No. 25
claims.source: Kaplan, Fighter Aces of the Luftwaffe in World War II (2007), pp. 49-50; the Internet Archive's lending copy, its text
claims.note: Kaplan: on fire, it exploded, "falling through the formation and colliding with another B-26". Of the three MACRs only No. 25's describes fire, and Baugher gives No. 25 to Galland. Which B-26 it struck, no record read says. From the book's text.

claims.question: Whose bombers and escort?
claims.answer: The 17th Bomb Group's B-26s, with P-47s of the 27th and 50th Fighter Groups
claims.source: Baker, Adolf Galland, the Authorised Biography (1996), pp. 284-88; the Internet Archive's lending copy, its text
claims.note: The MACRs agree on the group; the escort is Baker's. Baker has Galland's second bomber going "earthward in flames", Kaplan only "heavily damaging it". From the book's text.

claims.question: Who hit Galland?
claims.answer: Lt. James Finnegan, 50th Fighter Group, leading the P-47s' top cover flight, about 3,000 feet above the bombers
claims.source: Kaplan, Fighter Aces of the Luftwaffe in World War II (2007), pp. 49-50; the Internet Archive's lending copy, its text
claims.note: He dived on a jet banking left: Galland was banking steeply left when hit. One three-second burst from within 100 yards; claimed a "probable". From the book's text.

claims.question: How many bombers were lost?
claims.answer: Three that went down at once, and a fourth so badly damaged it crash-landed
claims.source: Ethell and Price, The German Jets in Combat (1979), pp. 54-55; the Internet Archive's lending copy, its text
claims.note: The three are the MACRs here. The fourth crash-landed, perhaps on our side of the lines, so perhaps with no MACR: still to identify. Ethell's "French-flown" is wrong for these three (17th Bomb Group, American crews). From the book's text.

claims.question: How did the jets attack?
claims.answer: Head-on first, then over the formation and round to attack from behind
claims.source: Ethell and Price, The German Jets in Combat (1979), p. 54
claims.note: Six jets from Riem, one turning back. Agrees with Galland ("fast auf Gegenkurs") and with No. 25's gunners, who saw it attacked "from 5 o'clock rear" and "from 6 o'clock level" (MACR 14164, pp. 4-5).

claims.note: Baugher gives no source for the pilot. Fits Galland's first victim (on fire, exploding: Kaplan) and No. 25's gunner, who saw it attacked from behind (MACR 14164, p. 5).

positions.label: Munich-Riem: JV 44's airfield
positions.note: The district of Riem; the wartime airfield is now built over (Messestadt Riem). JV 44 at Riem and its 1130 take-off are from secondary accounts (Forsyth's histories of JV 44, via The Aviation Geek Club), not a German record

positions.label: Lechfeld airfield: the bombers' briefed target
positions.note: Target or Intended Destination Lechfeld Ger. on all three forms (MACRs 14162-14164); drawn at today's Lechfeld air base (OpenStreetMap). Whether the group reached it and bombed is not in the records read

positions.label: Eichstätt
positions.note: On the 432nd's sketch of the formation's course

positions.label: Spot Cash's last known position: Neuburg
positions.note: Typed only as Neuburg, Ger. (last sighted); drawn at the town's centre. Course typed 70 Degrees Mag. A later pencil note beside it (340 mi S.E. of Frankfurt, and a latitude and longitude) is not used

positions.label: Two B-26s down south-east of here: map grid square T5026
positions.source: 45th Inf Div G-2 Periodic Report No. 219 p. 2
positions.note: The Army's maps were ruled in 1 km squares (the Nord de Guerre grid); a report could give the square, not a point, so the whole square is drawn, hatched. T5026 is the square as typed; decoded with tools/grid_ref.py (our decoding). Its south-west corner is about 100 m from Bergen; Big Red's last known position is 3.5 km south-east of it

positions.label: Rennertshofen: the division's CP from 1010
positions.note: The journal names the town only; drawn at its centre

positions.label: Ried: the 179th's 1st Bn shelled
positions.note: The grid as typed (RIED 537225) decoded with tools/grid_ref.py: 0.3 km from the village's centre

positions.label: Marxheim: the 157th's crossing
positions.note: The grid as typed (MARKHEIM (358200)) decoded with tools/grid_ref.py

positions.label: German anti-aircraft guns on wagons reported: map grid squares 5219 and 5220
positions.note: The 179th Infantry reported three flak (anti-aircraft) wagons, guns on rail or road carriages, somewhere in two 1 km squares of the Army's map grid: the south edge of Neuburg and the ground south of it. The squares as typed (vic 5220 and 5219), decoded with tools/grid_ref.py (our decoding); a US report of German guns

routes.label: Big Red (432nd Bomb Sq), its course at the last known position
routes.resolved: the course as typed, 155°, into Big Red's last known position; the line's length (6 km) is drawn, not recorded
routes.note: Course typed 155° beside the last known position, 48° 46′ N, 11° 11′ E, at 1150. Probably the crippled plane's own heading, not the formation's: a waist gunner saw it hit on the jets' first pass, nose up and fall "off to the left under partial control", last seen at about 8,000 feet (MACR 14163, p. 4); the 432nd's sketch has it "last seen out of control to south into clouds" (MACR 14162, p. 5).

routes.label: No. 25 (37th Bomb Sq), its course at the last known position
routes.resolved: the course as typed, 140°, into Neuburg an der Donau; the line's length (6 km) is drawn, not recorded
routes.note: Course typed 140 degrees, the last known position only "Neuberg, Germany", at 1152; drawn into the town's centre. The squadron's sketch (p. 6) puts the crash in the woods by Rohrenfels.

routes.label: Spot Cash (34th Bomb Sq), its course where last sighted
routes.resolved: the course as typed, 70°, into Spot Cash's last known position: Neuburg; the line's length (6 km) is drawn, not recorded
routes.note: Course typed "70 Degrees Mag.", last sighted over Neuburg at 1145. Drawn as if true: the magnetic variation, a degree or two here in 1945, is not applied. A bombardier in its flight saw a B-26 "under control, at approximately 5,000 feet with a P47 down with him. He was headed East in the area of Neuburg", not sure it was this one (MACR 14163, p. 18).

routes.label: The formation's course in, on the 432nd's sketch (the western dashed line)
routes.source: Missing Air Crew Report 14162, p. 5 (sketch map)
routes.note: "Course of formation", dashed, on a hand-drawn sketch with a ruled grid (1:500,000, 10′ squares). Traced on the grid; the sketch's own towns sit up to about 3 km from where they are (it draws Neuburg too far south), so the line is good to a few kilometres. Its arrowheads point south-south-east, towards Neuburg: the way in, on the courses the forms type at the attack (155°, 140°). Read with the statements (formation-sketch-b): ours.

routes.label: The formation's turn south of Neuburg and its course home, on the 432nd's sketch (the eastern dashed line)
routes.source: Missing Air Crew Report 14162, p. 5 (sketch map)
routes.note: The second dashed line, east of the first: a loop south of Neuburg, then north-north-west, its arrowheads pointing that way. Read as the turn after the attack and the way home (ours), from a bombardier's statement: "as we started our turn home immediately after the attack, I saw a B-26 under control, at approximately 5,000 feet with a P47 down with him. He was headed East in the area of Neuburg" (MACR 14163, p. 18, Lt. Edgar W. Seefield, 28 April 1945). The sketch's X (Big Red) sits by this line, not the first: a waist gunner saw it hit "on their first pass" and fall "off to the left under partial control" (MACR 14163, p. 4), so the X is where it went, not where the formation was. Traced on the grid as the first line, good to a few kilometres; drawn from the loop's western end.

routes.label: JV 44's Me 262s, Munich-Riem to Neuburg
routes.resolved: straight between two places: the path between them is not recorded
routes.source: The Aviation Geek Club, drawing on Robert Forsyth's histories of JV 44
routes.note: A straight line from the airfield to the fight: no record here gives the jets' route. The take-off at 1130 is from secondary accounts; the fight is at 1145-1152 by the MACRs and the 106th's history. The line can't show the approach: the 37th Bomb Squadron's witnesses have the jets attacking from behind, "in low from 5 o'clock rear" and "from 6 o'clock level" (MACR 14164, pp. 4-5), which on the formation's course of about 140-155° is from the north-west.

routes.label: The single Me 262 at 1725, north-east to south-west at 1,500 feet
routes.resolved: the course as typed, 225°, into Wellheim: the 106th AAA AW Bn's command post from 1515; the line's length (8 km) is drawn, not recorded
routes.source: 45th Infantry Division, G-2 Periodic Report No. 219, p. 2
routes.note: The course is the report's ("flying NE to SW over Div sector", 1,500 ft), taken as 225°; where it crossed is not given. Drawn through the 106th AAA AW Bn's command post at Wellheim (from 1515), since the battalion engaged it, so the line's place is ours: hence dotted, as inferred.

rings.label: Battery D's 37 mm guns, their reach (round Bergen, assumed)
rings.note: The 37 mm gun's maximum horizontal range "as limited by fuze or tracer", 3,500 yards (its vertical the same). The battalion fired "10 rounds 37mm and 159 rounds .50 cal." at the jets (its April history, p. 6). Centred on Bergen, where the 189th was from 1015: the battery's own place that day isn't recorded.

rings.label: Battery D's .50 caliber machine guns, their reach (round Bergen, assumed)
rings.note: The .50 caliber machine gun's "tracer range", 1,850 yards. Centred on Bergen, assumed, as the 37 mm ring.
